full_text:
**Verdict: KNOWN.** This is the Schelling segregation model on a lattice with vacancies, using blind random relocation. The three-colour version is a small variant, and I don't expect it to change the behaviour.

**1. Model family.** The system is a lattice of agents of kC=3 types plus empty sites. I read the primary rule as follows: an agent whose fraction of same-type neighbours is below 0.3 (`SAME_LT`, radius 1) jumps to a vacant site with probability 0.1. That is a Schelling-class relocation model, and every rule listed under "same class" is a threshold-triggered, probabilistic move to a vacant site.

**2. The behaviour in the literature.**
- **Earliest source.** Schelling (1969, 1971) is the origin. I did not retrieve either paper. I only saw secondary descriptions of them:
  - Schelling (1971) presented a two-dimensional version in which empty cells serve as destinations for relocating agents.
  - Schelling observed that this system always reached a segregated state with large same-colour clusters.
- **Physics-style treatment.** Gauvin, Vannimenus & Nadal, EPJ B 70, 293 (2009), arXiv:0903.4694, is the closest direct match:
  - Some sites are blank and agents of both colours may move to these vacancies.
  - Their phase diagram has a frozen state at low tolerance, a segregated state, and a mixed state at higher tolerance.
  - They also link the model to spin-1 models.
- **Reviews.**
  - Stauffer & Solomon (arXiv:0706.3983, a review-style paper) cover Schelling segregation and its relation to Ising and Potts models. They describe simulations with two and more groups.
  - The unified framework of arXiv:1104.1971 says the literature on the model's variants is fragmented.
- **Probabilistic, blind moves.** The "p=0.1 per step, move to a random vacancy" feature is standard:
  - Moves are "blind": the agent goes to a uniformly random vacant site.
  - In another formulation, any agent below the satisfaction threshold relocates at random to a vacant location.
  - Jones's variant added randomness and produced really large ghettos. I read Stauffer & Solomon as saying this randomness removes the blocking of cluster growth.
- **Three groups.** The three-colour case has also been studied. Fossett considered three residential groups (White, Black and Hispanic). I only saw a snippet of this source.

**3. What differs, and whether it matters.**
- **Three types instead of two.** The multi-group case is documented, so this is not new. With three types, a run could end in more than three domains. The Stauffer & Solomon review notes that with conserved group membership there is one domain per group at low-temperature equilibrium. The high `g_n_domains` (6.7) is therefore plausibly a coarsening or kinetic effect with finite vacancy and probabilistic moves. I did not find a source that quantifies it.
- **Move trigger.** The agent moves when it is unhappy, not only when the destination would make it happy. This matches the "blind move" variants cited above.
- **Negative activity trend (-4.9).** This is what you would expect as unhappy agents settle into clusters and the move rate falls. Gauvin et al. also describe frozen states in which no agent moves.
- **`NEXT_GE` and `CNT_LE` rules.** I did not look these up specifically. `CNT_LE(b=1, th=2)` appears to trigger on a count of one neighbour type, and `NEXT_GE(th=3)` on a count of a "next" type. These are not the standard same-fraction rule. They are probably still in the same segregation or avoidance class, but this is untested and I am inferring it from the rule names.
- **Why the fingerprint looks non-textbook.** The usual Schelling setting is two types, near-deterministic dynamics, and a fixed vacancy density. A low move probability (0.01–0.1), three types and many domains would all push the summary statistics away from textbook values. I read that as a parameter and kinetics difference, not a new phenomenon.

**4. Confidence: medium-high.** The Schelling model with vacancies is thoroughly documented, and the core behaviour (threshold-triggered relocation producing segregation into domains) is the textbook result. I am less sure of two things. First, I did not read a source that treats this exact probabilistic three-colour setup with the `NEXT_GE`/`CNT_LE` triggers. Second, I read the grammar from the rule names without a spec.

- Schelling segregation vacancies threshold
- Gauvin Vannimenus Nadal phase diagram
- Schelling more than two groups
- Schelling multiple groups, random move probability
